claims.text: The pre-exposure microstructure and native oxide state of Q235 steel govern whether a protective oxide layer forms during aggressive salt exposure.
Pre-exposure annealing refines the grain structure of Q235 steel.
Pre-exposure annealing homogenizes or adjusts the distribution of inclusions in Q235 steel.
The annealing-induced microstructure promotes rapid formation of a continuous, adherent iron-oxide layer during salt exposure at 700–900 °C.
A continuous, adherent iron-oxide layer retards further high-temperature corrosion.
As-received Q235 steel has a heterogeneous microstructure and native surface oxides before additional annealing.
Annealing favors more uniform oxide nucleation by modifying the Q235 microstructure.
The resulting high-temperature oxide layer limits salt penetration and oxidation.
Room-temperature oxide-scale formation is too kinetically limited to provide substantial protection through the proposed mechanism.
At room temperature, initial microstructural differences between annealed and non-annealed Q235 steel will not materially change protection.
Annealed Q235 steel will develop a more coherent protective oxide layer than non-annealed Q235 steel during high-temperature salt exposure.
Annealed Q235 steel will develop a thicker protective oxide layer than non-annealed Q235 steel during high-temperature salt exposure.
Annealed Q235 steel will have a lower corrosion rate than the non-annealed control during salt exposure at 700–900 °C.
The difference in corrosion protection between annealed and non-annealed samples will be minimal at room temperature.
The proposed mechanism should apply primarily during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C and should not produce a significant treatment effect at room temperature.
Annealed and untreated Q235 samples should be compared under both room-temperature and 700–900 °C aggressive salt exposure.
Oxide continuity, adhesion, thickness, phase composition, weight change, corrosion rate, and microstructure can be used to test the proposed mechanism.
